summary: The day lends itself to two checkable tasks, one on rebinding names and one on what and/or give back and which binds first; its layout, comment and input/output steps are conventions, typed input or printed output, and the one checkable piece of input/output (an aligned f-string) is the exercise's summary_line.

steps.title: Python syntax: blocks, lines and the layout PEP 8 asks for
steps.reason: The step teaches layout and naming conventions (indentation, continuation lines, 79 columns, blank lines, import order, snake_case), and a check sees names and values, never how the file is laid out. Its one behaviour, IndentationError, stops the run before any check is tried.

steps.title: Comments that earn their place
steps.reason: Comments are a convention: the tokenizer drops them, so no check can tell a why-comment from a stale one. A module docstring does reach __doc__, but the only wrong answer there is not writing one.

steps.title: Variables and datatypes: names bound to objects
steps.reason: Rebinding and the run-time evaluation of an f-string leave names whose values a check can read, and both mistakes the page names (expecting a copied name to follow a rebinding, building the f-string before the names change) give a different value. It has to be a short script, since functions are deferred to Friday, and it stays off the exercise's ten helpers.

steps.title: Operators: arithmetic, comparisons and boolean logic
steps.reason: What and/or give back and how and binds tighter than or show up in a bound value, and the page names both mistakes. The exercise and demo 02 already take //, hours left, the breach flag, the priority check, the chained comparison, % 3 and round, so the task works on the rule they leave out: an open ticket that was reopened or is high priority. Functions are deferred to Friday, so it is a short script that binds names and rebinds them for a second ticket.

steps.title: User input and output: print, format specs and the standard streams
steps.reason: print's sep, end and file, input() and the standard streams are printed output, typed input or the shell, none of which a check can see or the runtime offers. The one value a check could read, an aligned f-string row, is the exercise's summary_line acceptance criterion and the demo's board row.

tasks.title: Variables
tasks.idea: A short script about reassigning a ticket. Starting from assignee = "dana" and hours_open = 5.5, the reader keeps the current owner under previous, rebinds assignee to "lee", adds half an hour with +=, and then builds note = f"{previous} -> {assignee} at {hours_open}h", which ends as "dana -> lee at 6.0h".
checks: previous still holds "dana" after assignee is rebound to "lee"; binding previous after the rebinding gives "lee".
note reads "dana -> lee at 6.0h"; building the f-string before the rebinding or the += freezes the old values, because an f-string reads its names when its own line runs.
tasks.q: Write a short script that hands a ticket to a new owner. It starts with assignee = "dana" and hours_open = 5.5. Keep the current owner under the name previous, rebind assignee to "lee" and add half an hour to hours_open. Then build note with the f-string f"{previous} -> {assignee} at {hours_open}h", so that when the script ends note is "dana -> lee at 6.0h".
tasks.tests:
assert previous == "dana", "previous keeps the owner the ticket had first"
assert assignee == "lee", "assignee is bound to the new owner"
assert hours_open == 6.0, "hours_open has the extra half hour"
assert note == "dana -> lee at 6.0h", "note shows the handover and the hours as they end up"

tasks.title: Operators
tasks.idea: A short script. The starter binds one ticket as flat variables (is_open = True, reopen_count = 2, priority = "low"). The reader binds needs_escalation to one expression built from comparisons, and, or and parentheses: True when the ticket is open and has been reopened at least once or has priority "high". Then the reader rebinds the three names to a closed high-priority ticket and binds closed_high to the same expression, which must be False.
checks: needs_escalation is True itself for the open, reopened ticket; writing reopen_count or ... hands back the count 2, because or returns one of its operands.
closed_high is False for the closed high-priority ticket; leaving out the parentheses, as in is_open and reopen_count >= 1 or priority == "high", lets it through, because and binds tighter than or.
The three names end bound to the closed high-priority ticket, so closed_high was computed from the rebound names and not from typed-in values.
tasks.q: The starter binds one ticket: open, reopened twice, priority "low". Bind needs_escalation to one expression that is True when the ticket is open and has either been reopened at least once or has priority "high", and False otherwise. Then rebind the three names to a closed ticket (is_open = False, reopen_count = 0, priority = "high") and bind closed_high to the same expression. When the script ends, needs_escalation is True and closed_high is False. Comparisons, and, or and parentheses are enough.
tasks.tests:
assert needs_escalation == True, "an open ticket that was reopened gives True itself, not the count"
assert closed_high == False, "a closed ticket gives False, even at high priority"
assert is_open == False and reopen_count == 0 and priority == "high", "the three names end bound to the closed high-priority ticket"
